A parameter-sparse state-space framework for characterizing coastal dune-aquifer architecture from manual dipwell records

M. Hollingham

Draft --- 2026

# Abstract

**Study region:** Newborough Warren, Anglesey, Wales. This is a coastal dune aquifer on the Irish Sea, monitored by 88 manual dipwells over 21 years and one climate station.

**Study focus:** Dune-slack vegetation depends on water-table depth within a band a few tens of centimetres wide. Distributed flow models of dune sand, however, need conductivity and thickness fields that are costly and poorly constrained. We ask whether routine dipwell records alone can resolve dune-aquifer architecture. We couple hierarchical clustering of hydrograph dynamics to a three-term state-space model, with terms for recharge, atmospheric draw and head-dependent drainage towards a level the fit itself sets. The model is fitted at each well from monthly rainfall and temperature, without coring, hydraulic testing or flow-model calibration.

**New hydrological insights for the region:** Five hydrogeological clusters emerge, each with distinct mechanistic coefficients. Interception-corrected apparent storage coefficients converge across them, and the coastal forest cluster sits at the upper edge of the open-dune range. The behavioural contrasts are therefore consistent with surface and land-cover control rather than storage. The fit closes the mean balance to within 1.7% of losses. How the loss splits between drainage and evapotranspiration is not identified from heads alone: 45% drainage at the median well under the adopted model, and 31--55% from an independent water balance. It raises median iterative Nash--Sutcliffe efficiency from 0.38 to 0.83 over a linear benchmark. Near the eroding shore, a coastal-retreat gradient analysed in a companion paper accounts for about half of the decline of the most coast-proximal cluster and most of the western dune cluster's.

**Keywords:** coastal dune aquifer; dune slack; state-space model; apparent storage coefficient; groundwater characterization; coastal retreat

Highlights

-   Dune-aquifer architecture resolved from manual dipwells and one climate station
-   Water balance closes; its drainage--evaporation split is bounded, not identified
-   Iterative forecast skill rises from NSE 0.38 to 0.83 over a linear benchmark
-   Interception-corrected apparent storage is broadly uniform across clusters

# Plain-language summary

Dune slacks, the damp hollows between sand dunes, hold some of the most water-sensitive habitats in north-west Europe. Their plants each live within a band of summer water depth only a few tens of centimetres wide. At most sites the only record of that water is a set of pipes read by hand once a month. This paper asks whether such a record, with one nearby weather station, is enough to work out how a dune aquifer is built and how it behaves, without drilling or a detailed model of underground flow.

At Newborough Warren on Anglesey, 88 such pipes have been read for 21 years. Sorted by the shape of their records, they fall into five groups: a quick-responding eastern block beside the lake and on the open dune, a slower western block, and two groups under the pine plantation. A simple monthly model, in which rain raises the water table and evaporation and drainage lower it, describes each group with four numbers. Run month after month from the weather alone, it follows the water table far better than the same model without drainage: a typical score of 0.83 against 0.38, on a scale where 1 is perfect.

The amount of water the sand holds turns out to be much the same everywhere once the rain caught by the forest canopy is allowed for. The forest groups behave differently mainly because the trees intercept rain at the surface, not because the ground beneath them is different. How the water lost each year divides between drainage and evaporation cannot be read from water levels alone. The paper gives the model's answer beside three other readings, and says how far they disagree.

The western shore is eroding, and the water table near it is falling faster than inland. That coastal effect is the subject of a separate paper; here it is removed from each group's trend before anything is put down to climate.

The method needs only routine records, so other dune sites can use it. What it cannot show is how water moves from one part of a site to another; that needs measurements of the sand itself.

# 1. Introduction

[]{#introduction}Coastal dune slacks are among the most hydrologically sensitive habitats in north-west Europe. They are defined by a seasonally fluctuating water table, and that water table sits within a narrow envelope. The wet- and dry-slack vegetation communities of conservation interest occupy a band of summer-minimum depth only a few tens of centimetres wide (Davy et al., 2006; Curreli et al., 2013). The envelope is set by groundwater, not by surface management. The conservation status of a dune system therefore cannot be understood without a quantitative account of how its aquifer fills, stores and releases water. That account must cover how recharge enters the water table, how evaporative demand and lateral drainage remove it, and how these processes vary across the geomorphological range of the site.

Characterizing that architecture by conventional hydrogeological means is difficult in dune settings. Distributed groundwater models of the MODFLOW family require hydraulic conductivity fields, aquifer-thickness surfaces and boundary fluxes. These are expensive to measure and poorly constrained in unconsolidated, rapidly transmissive dune sand. At Newborough Warren itself, an earlier distributed-model effort encountered exactly these calibration difficulties (Betson et al., 2002). Slug and pumping tests sample only the immediate vicinity of a borehole. Interpolating a parameter field across a dune system of several square kilometres needs dense borehole networks, and these are rarely available.

Yet many dune sites are monitored, often over decades, by exactly the kind of low-cost instrumentation that distributed models cannot directly exploit: networks of manual dipwells read at monthly intervals, alongside a nearby meteorological station. This paper addresses a methodological question. Is that routine monitoring record, on its own, sufficient to resolve the hydrogeological architecture of a dune aquifer --- its storage, recharge sensitivity and drainage behaviour? And can it do so with enough spatial detail to support conservation interpretation, without recourse to coring, hydraulic testing or calibrated continuous-flow modelling?

We develop and demonstrate such a framework. Its core is a three-term state-space model (SSM) fitted independently at each well. The model partitions the monthly change in water-table position into three terms: a recharge term proportional to rainfall, an atmospheric-draw term proportional to potential evapotranspiration, and a head-dependent drainage term proportional to the height of the water table above a base level that is fitted with the other coefficients. It is the exponential-response model of transfer-function practice, written month by month. A companion methods paper (Hollingham, 2026c) sets out the model and tests how far its forecasts can be trusted, on recent years held back from the fit and on two older records; here the model is used as a characterization tool. The three fitted coefficients are interpretable: recharge sensitivity, atmospheric draw, and the rate at which the water table returns to its own mean. As forcing, they require only monthly rainfall and temperature from a single station.

Around this core we assemble a set of complementary, independently derived characterizations that cross-validate one another. First, hierarchical clustering of hydrograph *dynamics* partitions the network into spatially coherent hydrogeological units before any model is fitted. It uses a correlation-based distance that isolates temporal behaviour from absolute water-table elevation. This provides a structure that the mechanistic coefficients must then independently reproduce. A pattern-matching affinity analysis extends the classification to wells with shorter records and identifies the gradational transition zones between units.

Next, the SSM is benchmarked against a traditional linear model under iterative simulation. The spatial pattern of the predictive gain itself then becomes a non-invasive diagnostic of where head-dependent drainage governs the aquifer. A water-balance decomposition built directly from the fitted coefficients quantifies the recharge--loss partition at each cluster under identical climate forcing. An independent water-table-fluctuation estimate of the apparent storage coefficient, Sₐ (the "apparent specific yield" of Healy and Cook, 2002), tests whether the behavioural contrasts between units reflect genuine differences in subsurface storage, or boundary conditions imposed at the surface. Finally, interpolation of the per-well coefficients yields continuous maps of recharge sensitivity, atmospheric draw and drainage rate. It also yields a mean head surface with its associated flow field and, at each well, a water-balance residual that makes explicit where the three-term model closes.

Long-term trends near the coast also carry an external forcing. Where a shoreline is eroding, the seaward drainage boundary migrates landward and deepens the nearby water table independently of climate. That forcing is fitted and tested in a companion paper (Hollingham, 2026f); here it is removed from each cluster's summer-minimum decline before any remainder is discussed.

The framework is demonstrated at Newborough Warren, a coastal dune system on Anglesey, north-west Wales. The site has been monitored over twenty-one years by a network of eighty-eight dipwells (eighty-nine monitoring points, including the Llyn Rhos-Ddu lake gauge). The network spans the full geomorphological range of the site, from lake-margin and open-dune slacks to a mature coniferous plantation on the elevated landward flank. The density and length of this record make it an unusually well-suited proving ground. It is large enough to test whether the framework recovers structure that is independently visible in the raw hydrographs. It is also varied enough to span the contrast between a shallow, fast-cycling open dune and a slower-draining forested interior.

The objectives of this paper are therefore: (i) to apply the state-space model of Hollingham (2026c) as a characterization framework; (ii) to demonstrate that hydrograph-dynamics clustering, mechanistic SSM coefficients, model-benchmarking diagnostics, water-balance decomposition and apparent-storage estimation converge on a single, internally consistent picture of aquifer architecture; (iii) to map that architecture continuously across the site and identify where the three-term water balance closes and where it does not; and (iv) to assess the framework's transferability to other dune systems monitored by routine dipwell networks.

Two management interventions were undertaken at the site: dune scraping and a partial plantation clearfell. Their hydrological consequences are quantified separately within a before-after-control-impact design and are reported in a companion paper (Hollingham, 2026b). They are not treated here; the plantation enters only as a land-cover boundary condition on the aquifer characterization. The intervention dates --- the December 2017 clearfell and the dune-scrape years --- are the author's recollection, from twenty-one years monitoring the site. The April 2015 CEH36 scrape is separately documented. No documentary record of the operations has been obtained.

# []{#anchor}2. Study site

Newborough Warren occupies the south-western tip of the Isle of Anglesey in north-west Wales (Figure 1). The modern dune system is a late-Holocene feature. The present dunes developed over previously cleared agricultural land following storms in 1330 (Ranwell, 1958; Rhind et al., 2001). The site has no perennial surface drainage. Flow lines shown on later figures are DEM-derived flow-accumulation paths, included for spatial reference.

Weakly permeable glacial till underlies the dune field and forms the effective base of the sand aquifer. A bedrock ridge, demarked by the 20 m AOD contour, trends south-south-west to north-north-east. It forms the northern boundary of the study area and outcrops within the northern plantation. The hydrological study area is defined by the extent of the DEM-derived flow network and covers approximately 865 ha. The dipwell network spans a core zone of roughly 720 ha within it, lying entirely on the south-eastern flank of the ridge. Dune terrain on the north-western flank drains toward the Malltraeth estuary. It is hydrologically separate and is not considered here.

The substrate divides the aquifer south-east of the ridge into two contrasting blocks (Stratford et al., 2007). In the east, shallow sand over till and estuarine deposits constrains storage and produces a responsive, flashy water-table regime. In the west, deep aeolian sand has accumulated over a broader platform. This permits substantial groundwater storage and strongly buffered seasonal fluctuations. The present data do not resolve what causes this east--west contrast (Section 5.1). It may reflect two distinct substrate bodies. Alternatively, it may reflect a single estuarine-clay base that outcrops on the higher eastern and southern ground and dips beneath the surface toward Caernarfon Bay, thinning the sand column in the east and thickening it toward the south-west.

The aquifer discharges principally across the south-western foreshore of Caernarfon Bay and the southern and eastern coast of the Menai Strait. Llyn Rhos-Ddu, a small lake within the warren, acts as a near-fixed-head body. It is the dominant local drainage sink for the immediately adjacent wells. It receives groundwater throughout the year, because the regional water table maintains its head above the lake surface (Stratford et al., 2007).

The northern part of the study area is managed plantation dominated by mature Corsican pine. The plantation enters the present analysis solely as a land-cover boundary condition. Its canopy intercepts a fraction of incident rainfall before it reaches the ground. This interception is treated below as a modifier of the surface input to the forested clusters, not as a management variable. The dune-slack communities of the open system are classified under the National Vegetation Classification as SD15b (wet slack) and SD16 (dry slack). Their community-mean water-table levels (Curreli et al., 2013) provide the ecological reference frame for the site, but are not used analytically in this paper.

# 3. Data and methods

## 3.1 Groundwater and climate records

[]{#groundwater-and-climate-records}The primary observational dataset is a network of manually read dipwells. Water-table elevation is recorded at approximately monthly intervals. Each reading is taken at the end of the month and represents the water level for the month just ended. Readings are bucketed to a monthly timestamp by field convention: a reading on or before the fifteenth of a month is assigned to the preceding month, and a later reading to the same month. All monthly series therefore index the month to which the reading belongs, not the day on which it was taken. Of the full monitoring array, wells with sufficient record length form the reference network used for model fitting. The remaining wells, with shorter records, form an extended network classified by pattern matching (Section 3.3). Water levels are expressed both in metres above ordnance datum and, for the state-space model, as depth below the ground surface at each well.

Climate forcing is taken from the Royal Air Force Valley station. Monthly precipitation totals are used directly. Potential evapotranspiration (PET) is computed by the Thornthwaite method from monthly mean temperature and station latitude. The heat index is summed over the trailing twelve months rather than the calendar year, so that it is defined for a record that does not end in December. Thornthwaite PET is an empirical index of atmospheric evaporative demand. Unlike Penman--Monteith, it does not define a specific reference surface, and this property bears on the interpretation of the atmospheric-draw coefficient (Section 5.3). Rainfall and PET are monthly totals for the same calendar month as the water-table change they are aligned against. No rainfall lag is applied, consistent with the end-of-month measurement convention.

## 3.2 Hierarchical clustering of hydrograph dynamics

[]{#anchor}The reference network is partitioned into hydrogeologically distinct zones by agglomerative hierarchical clustering with Ward's minimum-variance linkage (Ward, 1963). The distance metric is the Pearson correlation distance between standardized well hydrographs. This metric compares the *shape* of the seasonal and inter-annual water-table dynamics and discards absolute elevation. Two wells that fluctuate in synchrony are treated as similar, whatever their mean water-table depth. The clustering therefore isolates the dynamic hydrogeological signature --- the timing and relative amplitude of filling and draining --- from the topographic offset between wells.

The number of clusters is selected by a dual-metric approach that combines two measures. The first is the Ward's merge-distance profile, which identifies the partition at which further agglomeration incurs a disproportionate increase in within-cluster variance. The second is the mean silhouette coefficient (Rousseeuw, 1987), computed on the same correlation distance, which favours partitions with well-separated, internally coherent groups.

Each cluster is then described by its seasonal amplitude: the range between the 10th and 90th percentiles of each well's monthly water level, with the median taken over the cluster's wells (Figure 6). Amplitude plays no part in forming the clusters or in choosing their number: the correlation distance discards it.

## 3.3 Network extension by Pearson affinity analysis

[]{#anchor-1}The primary classification, derived from the reference network, is extended to the wells with shorter records by Pearson affinity analysis. Unlike the mechanistic models, this stage operates on the raw observed time series, without model fitting. Each well's hydrograph is correlated against every cluster centroid, and the well is assigned to the cluster with which it correlates most strongly. The correlation delta between the assigned cluster and the next-strongest one classifies membership into tiers. The tiers distinguish core members, which have an unambiguous dominant affinity, from wells whose affinities to neighbouring clusters compete closely. A multi-cluster affinity flag identifies wells whose hydrographs are nearly equally well matched by several centroids. The spatial concentration of these flags delineates the gradational transition zones, where the boundaries between hydrogeological units are diffuse rather than sharp. The extended-network wells are classified for spatial completeness and are not used in the cluster-level mechanistic fits.

We also tested whether a well's cluster-mates can fill the months it was not read. Where two wells were both read, a straight line relating one to the other is fitted. That line then turns the donor's reading in a missing month into an estimate for the target.

To test this, we hid months that had been read and checked how well each method put them back. We did this twice, for two stretches of 54 months: one starting in March 2006, near the start of the record, and one ending with its last month. Every well read in at least 80 % of a stretch was a target. Its hidden months were filled in five ways: from the nearest well that correlates with it at r ≥ 0.95; from the best-correlated well; from the nearest well in the same cluster that meets the same threshold; from the median of its cluster; and from the SSM run on climate alone. To keep the test fair, each line was fitted only on months outside the hidden stretch (at least 48), the clusters were worked out again without the hidden months, and donors within 50 m of their target were left out as near-twins. Each method was scored by how far it missed the mean spring (March--May) water level of each hidden year. The method to use was chosen by a rule set before the test: the smallest median miss over both stretches.

We also asked whether the clusters held in the past. The Countryside Council for Wales (CCW) read some of today's wells from 1989 to 1996. We grouped those wells on their 1989--96 readings alone, by the method of Section 3.2, and compared the groups with today's clusters. Agreement was scored by the adjusted Rand index (0 for chance, 1 for identical) and checked against random groupings. By a rule set before the test, the clusters count as having held only if agreement beats chance (p \< 0.05) and at least two-thirds of the pairs of wells that share a cluster today were grouped together then. As a check on the method, the same wells were also grouped on their modern readings.

## 3.4 State-space model and the displacement formulation

[]{#anchor-2}The mechanistic core of the framework is the monthly linear-reservoir model of Hollingham (2026c), Model B in that paper. It relates the monthly change in water-table position to climate forcing and to the antecedent head. For a given well or cluster centroid, the model is

> Δh(t) = α_B + β₁·P(t) − β₂·PET(t) − β₃·h_disp(t−1)

where Δh(t) is the change in water-table position during month t, and P(t) and PET(t) are the month-t precipitation and potential-evapotranspiration totals. The three β coefficients are reported as positive quantities. β₁ (recharge sensitivity) is the water-table rise per unit rainfall. β₂ (atmospheric draw) is the decline per unit PET. β₃ (proportional drainage decay) is the fraction of a departure from the water table\'s own equilibrium level that drainage removes each month. α_B is the fitted intercept.

The drainage term is driven by the displacement above the datum at the start of the month, so the level at the start of a month sets that month's drainage. Using the level at its end, h(t), would regress the change on its own end-point:

> h_disp(t−1) = z₀ + h(t−1)

where h is the water-table position (negative below ground) and z₀ is a fixed reference level, 3.7 m below the ground surface. The model is fitted by ordinary least squares with an intercept. Because α_B absorbs any reference level, z₀ drops out of the fit: the level at which the fitted drainage is zero, z_B = z₀ − α_B/β₃, is fitted rather than assumed, and it lies near each well\'s own mean. A departure from that level shrinks by a factor (1 − β₃) each month, so its e-folding time, −1/ln(1 − β₃), is a mean-reversion time and a property of the record rather than a recession towards a physical floor. Positive drainage is imposed as a bound on β₃, which the record does not identify everywhere. Hollingham (2026c, Sections 2.2 and 5.3) derives the model as a monthly step of the standard exponential-response model, sets out what the fitted base is and is not, and reports a fixed drainage floor at 3.7 m and at mean high water as the tested alternative that was not adopted (Section 7 there).

The recharge sensitivity of each unit is summarized by the lumped catchment storage coefficient, LCSC = 100/β₁. This is the depth of rainfall required to raise the water table by 100 mm. A lower LCSC denotes greater recharge sensitivity. LCSC/100 = 1/β₁ is itself an apparent storage coefficient: the rain needed per unit rise, as the water-table-fluctuation Sₐ is the recharge per unit rise (Section 3.8). The fitted coefficients fold together vegetation effects, storage and soil-moisture dynamics. For this reason, the recharge term in an open-boundary system of this kind can absorb unmeasured boundary fluxes into β₁ (Young, 2011; Knotters and van Walsum, 1997). This is addressed through the residual analysis (Section 3.10) and the Sₐ estimation (Section 3.8).

A depth-dependent extension was evaluated at cluster level as a diagnostic of depth coupling (Section 5.2). In it, β₂ is replaced by β₂·exp(−d_w/L_E), so that atmospheric draw declines as the water-table depth d_w increases, and L_E is found by grid search, as its reciprocal 1/L_E. The fixed-β₂ model is used throughout, as an effective depth-averaged parameterization.

The model is fitted at two scales, each on a declared record. The mechanistic characterization (Table 1) is fitted to each cluster-mean hydrograph on its full record. Averaging suppresses single-well noise and returns one coefficient set per zone. A cluster coefficient is therefore a centroid rather than a property of every member, and it depends on the partition. The per-well coefficients are fitted on the same 98 calendar months at every well, January 2018 to February 2026, so that wells are compared under the same climate. A month in which a well was found dry stays in the window as a level at or below the deepest the dipwell can read, not as a gap. These are the coefficients behind the coefficient ranges (Table 5), the coefficient surfaces (Figures 11--13) and the benchmark (Section 3.5). The per-well drainage timescales (Figure 14) are instead fitted on each well\'s full record, because the slow forest recession is not resolved within 98 months. How much record the drainage coefficient needs before it stabilizes, cluster by cluster, is reported by Hollingham (2026c, Section 4.3).

## 3.5 Model benchmarking against a traditional linear model

[]{#anchor-3}The predictive value of the head-dependent drainage term is assessed against a traditional linear model (TLM). The TLM is the same model without the drainage term and with a free intercept. It is fitted at every reference well on the 98-month comparison window and run freely over the same months from the first observed level, so the test is in-sample. Hollingham (2026c) sets out the models, the protocol and the network results, both for the no-intercept form used here and for the free-intercept form. The benchmark tests the drainage term against its absence. It does not choose between the two forms of the SSM, which are compared out of sample in the same paper. Here, the per-well gain in iterative Nash--Sutcliffe efficiency of the SSM over the TLM is mapped across the network (Figure 10). The map is a diagnostic of where the drainage term is indispensable to prediction and where the aquifer approximates a linear climate response.

## 3.6 Spatial coefficient mapping and within-forest regression

[]{#anchor-4}The per-well SSM coefficients are interpolated across the site by inverse-distance weighting. The interpolation runs over a regular grid built on a LiDAR-derived digital elevation model, with ridge cells and non-aquifer areas masked. The result is a set of continuous surfaces of recharge sensitivity, atmospheric draw and drainage rate, together with a model-fit-quality surface. These surfaces give a spatially resolved expression of aquifer behaviour that complements the cluster-level summaries.

Within the forested zone the per-well coefficients span much of the site-wide range. There, they are regressed against elevation, distance from the ridge and easting, and against canopy density measured at each well from the aerial imagery (Section 4.8). The regression tests whether the within-forest variation tracks topographic position and water-table depth, or canopy differences. The subsurface beneath the plantation is not cored, so elevation and position serve as proxies for substrate. The regression thus isolates this topographic control on the mechanistic coefficients beneath a single land cover.

## 3.7 Mean monthly water-balance decomposition

[]{#mean-monthly-water-balance-decomposition}The fitted cluster coefficients are used to decompose the mean monthly water balance of each cluster into its component fluxes, under identical climate forcing. Recharge is computed as β₁ times mean monthly precipitation. Atmospheric draw is β₂ times mean monthly PET. Drainage is β₃ times the mean height of the water table above the base level that the model fits for each cluster (Section 3.4). All terms are expressed in metres of water-table change per month, the natural unit of the state-space model. They are directly comparable across clusters that receive the same climate input. The model is fitted on gross rainfall and above-canopy PET, so at the forested clusters the canopy's interception loss (24% of rainfall; Freeman, 2008, a single-plot, single-season measurement and the only site value) is already inside the evaporation term. It is shown as part of the evaporation and never added to the losses. The net monthly balance is recharge minus total losses. It quantifies the residual that would be required from an unmeasured boundary input to maintain long-run equilibrium.

An indicative volumetric conversion is presented alongside the head-space decomposition. It applies each cluster's head-space split to the full rainfall, so it needs no storage coefficient. The split between evapotranspiration and drainage is not identified from heads alone (Hollingham, 2026c). It is quoted from Model B. Beside it are a depth-dependent variant and the ratio of winter to summer recession rates. Two readings that need neither form are reported with them: the floor that the water balance puts under drainage, and the water-balance residual analysis of Hollingham (2026c) (Section 4.5).

## 3.8 Apparent storage coefficient by the water-table-fluctuation method

[]{#anchor-5}An independent estimate of storage, the apparent storage coefficient Sₐ, is derived from the dipwell record by the water-table-fluctuation method (Healy and Cook, 2002). It is not the specific yield Sy of the sand: it lumps drainable porosity with the state of the capillary fringe and drainage within the month. In this method, Sₐ is the ratio of net recharge to the corresponding water-table rise. The method is applied to the cluster-mean hydrographs. It retains only months in which both the water table rose and net recharge was positive above defined thresholds, and it constrains event-level estimates to a physically plausible range. Monthly data cannot isolate individual storm events. At monthly resolution, the method is also known to conflate gravity drainage with capillary-fringe release. The resulting estimates are therefore interpreted as upper bounds on effective storage rather than as point estimates (Healy and Cook, 2002; Scanlon et al., 2002).

For the forested clusters, a canopy-interception correction is applied to the precipitation term before net recharge is computed: unlike the decomposition of Section 3.7, the method takes rainfall as recharge directly, so interception must be removed from it. The correction reduces only the rainfall input and leaves the Thornthwaite PET term unchanged. PET is an energy-based atmospheric-demand index, independent of land cover. Reducing it to account for canopy-evaporated interception would conflate atmospheric demand with realized evapotranspiration, and would remove the same quantity from both sides of the balance. The corrected forest estimates are compared against the open-dune range. The comparison tests whether the attenuated water-table response beneath the canopy reflects the surface boundary condition or a genuinely different subsurface storage. The per-well event-median Sₐ values are interpolated across the site. This assesses whether the spatial distribution of storage is uniform or shows discontinuities coinciding with the cluster margins.

## 3.9 Coastal-retreat correction

Summer-minimum trends near the eroding Caernarfon Bay shoreline carry a deepening that climate does not explain. Its network-scale gradient, a Dupuit drawdown from the migrating shoreline with amplitude δ₀ and inland reach L_cg, is fitted and tested in a companion paper (Hollingham, 2026f). Here the fitted gradient is used only to separate each cluster's coastal component from the rest of its decline (Section 4.11). The coastal term of each cluster is the mean, over its wells, of the gradient at each well's own distance from the shore.

## []{#anchor-6}3.10 Spatial interpolation, flow field and water-balance residual

The mean water-table surface is built by ordinary kriging of each well's mean head with a spherical variogram. Kriging is the geostatistical approach generally preferred over deterministic interpolators, such as inverse-distance weighting, for mapping groundwater levels from sparse wells (Varouchakis and Hristopulos, 2013; Rao et al., 2022). Kriging admits a drift on the ground surface (Desbarats et al., 2002), but here the drift was tested rather than assumed. Three drifts were compared with ordinary kriging by leave-one-well-out error and by a physical test against Sentinel-2 wet-floor extents, and ordinary kriging was selected (Hollingham, 2026d, §3.8). The edges are anchored rather than extrapolated. Seaward, the anchor is the sea along the high-water mark, at a coastal head fitted to the coastal wells between mean tide level and mean high water (UKHO, 2026). Inland, the anchors are the Afon Braint, Llyn Rhos-Ddu and the ridge well CEH12. No elevation mask is applied. Flow arrows are the negative head gradient, one per 100 m square, sized by the gradient. No hydraulic conductivity or aquifer thickness enters them. They describe the flow geometry of the mapped surface rather than the output of a calibrated continuous-flow model (Bear, 1972; Freeze and Cherry, 1979).

The water-balance residual quantifies, at each reference well, the degree to which the three-term SSM closes the long-term water balance. It is computed from the fitted coefficients as the difference between modelled mean losses (atmospheric draw plus drainage) and modelled mean recharge. Gross rainfall is used at every well; interception is already in β₂·PET̄ (Section 3.7). Positive residuals indicate locations where modelled losses exceed modelled recharge. This points to an inadequacy in the three-term model at that location, or in principle to an unmodelled input. Near-zero residuals indicate that the three-term balance closes adequately. The residual is shown at the wells alone and is not interpolated. Left out one well at a time, no interpolator predicts a withheld well's residual appreciably better than the network mean, so no surface is drawn. The residual is interpreted as a structural diagnostic of where the model's three terms are sufficient, not as a quantified map of lateral inflow. This is because it also absorbs nonlinear soil-moisture storage dynamics, coefficient sensitivity and any systematic bias in the Thornthwaite PET estimate. The mechanistic attribution of the residual pattern is tested in two ways. An independent cross-correlation lag analysis tests for distance-dependent transport from the ridge. A seasonal climatology analysis tests for unmodelled summer evaporative demand.

## 3.11 Computational implementation

[]{#data-and-methods}[]{#computational-implementation}All data pre-processing, statistical modelling and spatial mapping were implemented as a sequential, numbered Python pipeline. Time-series management used pandas and NumPy, and model fitting used statsmodels. Spatial interpolation and rendering were carried out over a LiDAR DEM. The state-space alignment and the drainage term are implemented once, in a shared model-utilities module. Every script that fits the SSM calls this module, which ensures that all downstream analyses are consistent with the cluster-level fits. The pipeline and its outputs are reproducible by running the published scripts in sequence.

# []{#anchor-7}4. Results

## []{#anchor-7}4.1 Climate and well-network characterization

The RAF Valley record establishes that Newborough Warren operates under a persistent annual water surplus. Over the monitoring period, mean annual precipitation was approximately 891 mm and mean annual Thornthwaite PET approximately 652 mm, a study-period P/PET ratio of about 1.36 (Figure 2). The surplus is strongly seasonal. Winter rainfall exceeds evaporative demand by a wide margin. In summer, PET exceeds rainfall, so atmospheric demand on the aquifer is concentrated in the period of lowest recharge. Year-to-year variability in the water balance is driven almost entirely by precipitation, not by evaporative demand. Evaporative demand shows strong seasonality and a small positive inter-annual trend (1.96 mm/yr over 2007--2025), but it varies by only about 3% about its mean, against about 19% for winter rainfall. The post-2013 period has run warmer than the earlier summer-temperature baseline (Figure 3), which intensifies the summer deficit.

The reference network comprises 66 wells with monthly water-table records over the 2005--2026 monitoring period. It is supplemented by 22 extended-network wells with shorter records, classified by pattern matching (Section 4.3). The median record length is well above a decade. This gives the spatial density needed to distinguish cluster-scale behaviour from site-wide climate forcing.

## []{#anchor-8}4.2 Network clustering and spatial architecture

Hierarchical clustering resolves five spatially coherent units under the dual-metric selection of k (Figure 4). The clustering used the standardized hydrograph dynamics, the Pearson correlation distance and Ward's linkage. The partition separates the network into a lake-margin unit (C1, Lake Edge), an open-dune unit (C2, Dune) and a western unit on deeper sand (C3, Western Residual). Two further units lie beneath the Corsican pine plantation and are distinguished by topographic position: C4, Main Forest, on the elevated ridge flank, and C5, Coastal Forest, on the lower coastal fringe (Figure 5). The cluster sizes are C1 = 7, C2 = 19, C3 = 26, C4 = 9 and C5 = 5 wells.

The five units recover the broad substrate contrast between the responsive, storage-limited east and the buffered, deeper-sand south-west (Stratford et al., 2007). The south-western unit (C3) is gradational toward both the open dune and the forest, rather than a sharply bounded block. The top Ward merge (linkage distance ≈0.99) separates C4 Main Forest from the other 57 wells. The east--west division, C1 and C2 against C3 and C5, follows at ≈0.61. C5 Coastal Forest therefore joins the western group rather than C4, despite sharing the pine canopy. Figure 6 shows the cluster-centroid hydrographs and seasonal amplitudes.

## 4.3 Affinity validation of the cluster structure

[]{#anchor-9}The Pearson affinity analysis supports the primary membership of 60 of the 66 reference wells. Membership falls into tiers, set by the correlation delta between the assigned cluster and the next-strongest one. A minority of wells are core members, with an unambiguous dominant affinity. Many others show closely competing affinities between neighbouring units. This is consistent with gradational rather than sharp boundaries in a contiguous, highly transmissive sand aquifer (Rao and Srinivas, 2006). Multi-cluster-affinity flags are concentrated along the C1/C2/C3 transition and the forest--dune margin. This concentration identifies the zones where geological and vegetative controls overlap.

**Filling gaps from cluster-mates.** Copying from the nearest well in the same cluster did best, and was adopted. Over both 54-month test stretches it missed the hidden spring levels by a median 0.041 m, against 0.139 m for the SSM run on climate alone (Figure 7a). The early stretch (from March 2006, including the unexplained high water of 2006--08; Hollingham, 2026c) was harder for both: 0.065 against 0.149 m; the late stretch (to the end of the record) gave 0.037 against 0.132 m. The nearest well from any cluster (0.041 m) and the best-correlated well (0.043 m) did almost as well; the cluster median did worse (0.059 m). The further the donor, the larger the miss (Figure 7b; Spearman ρ = +0.61).

With that method, 69 wells gain 4,432 filled months, and 37 gaps have no suitable donor and stay empty. Filled months are marked as such and are not used anywhere else in this paper.

The clusters did not hold in 1989--96 by the rule (Figure 7c). Grouped on their early readings, the 12 CCW wells agree with today's clusters no better than chance (adjusted Rand index 0.03, p = 0.45), and only 28 % of the pairs that share a cluster today were grouped together then. Grouped on their modern readings, the same wells match today's clusters well (0.75), so the small number of wells is not the reason. The difference lies with three warren wells near the sea (NW6, NW5 and WMC2, now in C3). NW3 and NW4 (now C2) keep each other's company in both periods, as do NW11 and NW13 (C3); the three seaward wells moved with the first pair in 1989--96 and with the second today. Many early readings sit at the bottom of the pipe, below which the water table cannot be read. Keeping those readings raises the agreement to 0.20, and using only the 10 least-affected wells gives 0.17; neither passes the rule. The test therefore does not show that the clusters held, but with twelve wells over seven years it cannot show that they changed either.

## 4.4 Cluster mechanistic coefficients

The model, fitted to each cluster-centroid hydrograph, characterizes the five clusters mechanistically (Table 1). Every coefficient is significant at every cluster except the drainage coefficient at C4 Main Forest (p = 0.447), which the record does not identify.

**Table 1.** Cluster mechanistic characterization. β₁ = recharge sensitivity (mm rise per mm rainfall); β₂ = atmospheric draw (mm decline per mm PET); −β₃ = proportional drainage decay (the fraction of a departure from the cluster\'s own fitted base level recovered each month); LCSC = 100/β₁, the reciprocal of β₁ (mm of rainfall per 100 mm of water-table rise); R² = one-step diagnostic fit.

  --------------------- --------- ------- ------- ------- ---------- -------
  Cluster               n wells   β₁      β₂      −β₃     LCSC (%)   R²
  C1 Lake Edge          7         3.715   3.144   0.354   26.918     0.818
  C2 Dune               19        3.500   2.619   0.167   28.571     0.789
  C3 Western Residual   26        3.604   2.126   0.103   27.749     0.832
  C4 Main Forest        9         2.578   2.499   0.010   38.790     0.733
  C5 Coastal Forest     5         2.463   1.335   0.045   40.609     0.706
  --------------------- --------- ------- ------- ------- ---------- -------

[]{#cluster-mechanistic-coefficients}Recharge sensitivity β₁ is highest at the Lake Edge (C1: 3.715), with the Western Residual (C3: 3.604) and the Dune (C2: 3.500) close behind it. Each millimetre of rainfall therefore drives a comparable water-table rise across the open dune. The two forested clusters return substantially lower recharge sensitivities (C4: 2.578, C5: 2.463), consistent with canopy interception suppressing the rainfall signal that reaches the water table. Expressed as LCSC (100/β₁), 27--29 mm of rainfall raises the water table by 100 mm across the open dune, against 39--41 mm beneath the plantation. Beneath the canopy, roughly 40% more rain is therefore needed for the same rise.

Atmospheric draw β₂ is highest at the Lake Edge (C1: 3.144), where the water table stands shallowest, and lowest at the Coastal Forest (C5: 1.335). The Dune (C2: 2.619) and the forest interior (C4: 2.499) follow, and the Western Residual (C3: 2.126) is lower than either. C5 carries the same pine canopy as C4 yet returns little more than half its atmospheric draw, so the canopy alone does not set the cluster-level contrast. Within the forest, β₂ follows elevation and water-table depth (Section 4.8), which points to topographic position rather than canopy as the dominant control.

The drainage decay −β₃ shows the strongest contrast of the three coefficients. It is highest at C1 (0.354), where rapid lateral exchange with Llyn Rhos-Ddu drives fast recovery. It falls through C2 (0.167) and C3 (0.103) to C5 (0.045). At C4 the centroid fit returns 0.010, but the record does not identify it, so the forest interior is reported as the cluster whose drainage the record cannot resolve rather than as the slowest (Hollingham, 2026c, Section 5.2).

## []{#anchor-10}4.5 Water balance and apparent storage

The head-space water-balance decomposition (Table 2; Figure 8a) closes to within 1.7% of total losses at every cluster, and within 0.6% outside C5. This closure is a property of the fit, not independent evidence. A model fitted to heads alone can be expected to close the mean balance (Hollingham, 2026c). The closure therefore shows that the three terms are mutually consistent at the cluster mean without an unmeasured boundary term. It does not show that each flux is confirmed. Recharge is highest at C1 (0.276 m/month) and lowest under the plantation (0.183--0.192 m/month). Total losses track recharge closely at every cluster.

How the loss divides between drainage and atmospheric draw is not identified from heads alone (Hollingham, 2026c). It is quoted here from Model B, the form used for every coefficient. Under Model B, drainage takes 38% of the loss at C1, 45% at C2, 56% at C3 and 61% at C5. At C4 Model B's drainage coefficient is not significant (p = 0.45), so its share there is not identified; Tables 2 and 3 give it by difference, marked †.

Drainage is β₃ times the height above each cluster's fitted base level. The drainage/ET split is not identified from heads alone (Section 4.5). At C4, Model B's β₃ is not significant (p = 0.45), so its drainage and split (†) are taken by difference, recharge less atmospheric draw, and are not estimates of β₃.

The volumetric conversion (Table 3) places every cluster under 889--893 mm/yr of rainfall. At the forested clusters canopy interception removes ≈214 mm/yr, leaving 678--679 mm/yr of throughfall. Split by Model B, drainage runs from 340 mm/yr at C1 to 545 mm/yr at C5; at C4 it is not identified. Evapotranspiration after interception runs from 133 mm/yr at C5 to 553 mm/yr at C1. A forest's total evaporative loss is I + ET: 347 mm/yr at C5, against 488 mm/yr at C2. The split is least certain at C1, where the three estimators of Figure 8b span 38--60% drainage, and most certain at C3 (56--66%).

**Figure 8.** Water-balance decomposition by cluster: (a) the mean monthly head-space balance under Model B (recharge against atmospheric draw and drainage); (b) the indicative volumetric partition. In (b), the hatched band spans the ET/drainage split given by Model B, a depth-dependent variant and the ratio of winter to summer recession rates; it shows how far the split depends on the reading and is not a statistical confidence interval. Forest interception is part of the evaporation, not added to it (Section 3.7).

The WTF estimates of Sₐ (Table 4; Figure 9) provide an independent test. They ask whether the cluster contrasts reflect storage architecture or surface boundary conditions. Uncorrected, the forested-cluster event-median Sₐ values sit above the top of the open-dune range (C4: 0.321, against an open-dune maximum of 0.312; C5: 0.364). This is because gross rainfall overstates the recharge flux beneath the canopy. Applying the canopy-interception correction to the recharge term brings the cluster-level event medians down to 0.256 (C4) and 0.316 (C5). C4 then falls cleanly into the open-dune range (0.210--0.312), while C5 sits just above its upper edge. Aggregating instead as the median of the per-well estimates gives 0.253 and 0.308. The two aggregations are reported separately throughout and are not interchangeable. The β₁ route gives the same reading independently: LCSC/100 (the lumped catchment storage coefficient of Section 3.4) for the open-dune clusters (Table 1) lies inside their WTF range, and at the forested clusters, scaled to throughfall, it falls in that range too.

The correction uses a single literature fraction rather than a fitted one, so the convergence is tested against that fraction directly. The forest clusters' event medians were re-evaluated over interception fractions from 0 to 0.40 (Section 3.8). Both fall within the open-dune range only for fractions between 0.28 and 0.32: C4 for every fraction up to 0.32, C5 only from 0.28. The C4 result therefore does not depend on the particular value 0.24, while C5 sits just outside the range at that value. For C4 this is reassuring: its convergence holds whatever fraction is assumed. C5 converges only if the canopy intercepts more than the measured quarter, so its convergence is not shown. The seasonal residual analysis of Section 5.4 is an independent check, and its cross-cluster ordering is likewise inconsistent with a mis-set fraction.

Across the three open-dune clusters, the per-well Sₐ values are well described by a planar spatial trend (n = 52, R² = 0.610, residual standard deviation 0.031). Sₐ rises by 0.070 per kilometre along an azimuth of 231°, so storage increases steadily toward the south-west. Both components are significant (easting −0.054 per kilometre, northing −0.044 per kilometre, each p \< 0.001). The trend is fitted to, and reported for, the open-dune network only. The forested wells lie outside its spatial domain, and the surface is not extrapolated beneath the plantation.

The C4 result indicates that the attenuated water-table response beneath the plantation reflects the surface canopy boundary condition rather than a fundamentally different substrate. The C5 estimate is the least reliable in the network. A majority of its rising-limb events imply an event-level Sₐ at or above the porosity of dune sand. Its median is therefore constrained by the physical-plausibility limit rather than freely estimated, and it is reported as a weak corroborator only. All Sₐ medians are two to three times the specific yield of dune sand in the literature (0.08--0.12), the values assumed in Table 4. They are apparent storage, not a property of the sand, and are read as upper bounds (Healy and Cook, 2002; Scanlon et al., 2002).

## []{#anchor-11}4.6 Model benchmarking: SSM versus traditional linear model

Run freely over the comparison window, the SSM raises the median iterative Nash--Sutcliffe efficiency from 0.38 under the TLM to 0.83 across the 64 wells fitted on the window (Hollingham, 2026c, Section 4.1). It returns a positive efficiency at all 64, against 53 for the TLM. The gain holds when the floor is fixed (Hollingham, 2026c, Section 7). It is not uniform across the network (Figure 10). It is largest in the lake-proximal C1 Lake Edge, where head-dependent drainage is strongest (cluster median +1.02, against +0.51 at C2 and +0.31 at C3; e.g. CEH6: TLM −1.22 → SSM 0.89). It is smallest under the forest (+0.26 at C4 and +0.28 at C5). At one well, in the coastal forest, the SSM scores below the TLM. The spatial pattern of the gain therefore serves as a non-invasive diagnostic of where head-dependent drainage governs the aquifer.

Two readings constrain the split without either form. The first is a floor. Actual evapotranspiration cannot exceed PET, and over 21 years the mean change in storage is negligible. Drainage is therefore at least the excess of rainfall over PET: 237--239 mm/yr in the open dune (C1--C3). Model B's drainage there, 340--502 mm/yr (Table 3), lies above it, as does its 545 mm/yr at the coastal forest (C5).

The second is a water balance that takes storage from outside the fit (Hollingham, 2026c). Rainfall less PET is a monthly surplus. The change in storage is the water-table change times the well's apparent storage coefficient, Sₐ, from the water-table-fluctuation method (Section 3.8). What the surplus does not account for is taken as drainage. Over the 66 reference wells it puts drainage at 31% of the annual loss at the median well, against 45% under Model B. It books more of the loss to the atmosphere than Model B: 0.74 to 0.97 of PET as actual evapotranspiration, cluster by cluster. The reading depends on Sₐ. Estimated from winter months instead, Sₐ is bracketed by two regressions, of the water-table change on rainfall and of rainfall on the change (0.14--0.19 and 0.25--0.30 across the clusters), and the median share runs from 36% to 55%. Model B's 45% lies inside that bracket. The ratio of winter to summer recession rates, a share of summer recession rather than of the annual loss, gives 60, 35, 66, 51 and 73% at C1--C5. These are checks on the share, not revised drainage rates. None of them replaces a measured flux.

![](Pictures/10000000000006400000048B7A7A5B76.jpg){width="16.164cm" height="13.0322cm"}**Figure 10.** Iterative Nash--Sutcliffe gain of Model B over the traditional linear model at each reference well, interpolated across the network and masked over the dune ridges (colour scale capped at 1.5); the models and the free-running protocol are set out in Hollingham (2026c).

## []{#anchor-12}4.7 Spatial coefficient structure and drainage timescales

Interpolating the per-well coefficients yields continuous surfaces (per-well ranges in Table 5; Figures 11--13). Their broad structure aligns with the cluster boundaries, and they preserve substantial within-cluster variation. Recharge sensitivity β₁ is highest in the north-east around the Lake Edge wells (per-well up to 4.93). It declines across the open dune to its lowest values beneath the forest. Atmospheric draw β₂ peaks in the C4 forest interior and along the ridge-adjacent northern dune, and is lowest in the Coastal Forest. Drainage rate β₃ shows the strongest spatial contrast of any coefficient. It runs from the fast-draining Lake Edge (per-well up to 0.415 per month) to the near-stagnant forest interior. There, one ridge-flank well (CEH14) returns a fitted base above the ground surface, where the model does not capture the boundary condition.

The drainage coefficient sets how fast a departure from a well\'s own level decays. Figure 14 maps the mean-reversion time 1/β₃ across the network: the number of months over which a departure decays to about a third of its size. The timescale is a property of the record, not a recession towards a physical floor, and the record returns the same timescale without any model at all (Hollingham, 2026c, Section 4.7). It is not a bound on amplitude: over a summer, drainage removes only a small part of a winter excess even where the timescale is short, and the much larger seasonal fall is set by evapotranspiration (the β₂ term).

The spatial pattern follows β₃ (Figure 13). The eastern open dune recovers fastest, the western dune is intermediate, and the forest interior slowest of all, though the drainage coefficient is not identified there, at the centroid or at the wells ringed in Figure 14, so their times are not estimates. C5 Coastal Forest resembles the western dune despite sharing the pine canopy, which reinforces the substrate and elevation control. Mean-reversion times per cluster, with the model and without it, are tabulated by Hollingham (2026c, Table 3).

![](Pictures/100000010000075D0000061E2DE81B46.png){width="15.871cm" height="12.8435cm"}**Figure 14.** Mean-reversion time 1/β₃ (months, log scale) across the reference network, from each well\'s full-record fit under Model B. C4 Main Forest wells are ringed: Model B does not identify their drainage coefficient, so their times are not estimates. CEH13 (near-zero β₃) and CEH14 (drainage not defined) are excluded.

## 4.8 Substrate control within the forested zone

Within the forested zone the per-well coefficients span much of the site-wide range. Regression against elevation, distance from the ridge and easting identifies the underlying control (Table 6). Atmospheric draw β₂ is overwhelmingly governed by elevation (r = 0.964, p \< 0.001; R² = 0.929): higher wells on the ridge return systematically higher β₂. Drainage β₃ falls with elevation (r = −0.818, p \< 0.001). Both also vary with easting (β₂: r = 0.705, p = 0.005; β₃: r = −0.563, p = 0.037), though less strongly than with elevation. Distance from the ridge carries the same signal --- it correlates with both coefficients --- but adds almost nothing to either regression once elevation is in it (marginal R² gain 0.005 for β₂ and 0.001 for β₃), so elevation is the predictor these data support. Recharge β₁ shows no significant relationship with elevation (p = 0.63), with distance from the ridge (r = −0.435, p = 0.12) or with easting (r = 0.479, p = 0.083).

β₂ does vary substantially across clusters (Table 1), but the cluster-level contrast is set by substrate, water-table depth and topographic position rather than by canopy maturation: the C4--C5 split, a 2-fold difference in atmospheric draw within the plantation, is the cleanest evidence. C4 and C5 form two distinct groups rather than a continuum. They separate almost entirely on β₂ --- C4 at 2.10--4.21, C5 at 1.03--1.82, with no overlap --- and on mean elevation (C4: 10.6 m, C5: 5.6 m; p = 0.0001), corresponding to the transition from the elevated ridge flank, with its deeper water table and unsaturated zone, to the low coastal fringe, with a shallower water table. The canopy is not uniform. Its density was measured at each forest well from the dated aerial imagery, as a canopy texture index (0 for open ground, 1 for mature conifer) in a 30 m disc around the well, on the frames before the 2017 felling. Across the fourteen wells the index ranges from 0.15 to 1.47, yet it is not significantly related to β₂ (r = 0.26, p = 0.37) or to elevation (r = 0.25, p = 0.39), while β₂ follows elevation (partial r = 0.989 given the canopy index). Holding elevation constant, canopy adds nothing (partial r = 0.09, p = 0.77), and the result is the same with 20 m and 50 m discs. C4 and C5 do not differ in canopy (medians 0.99 and 0.82). The C4--C5 separation therefore tracks elevation and water-table depth rather than canopy. The subsurface beneath the plantation is not cored; on the topographic and coefficient evidence the C4/C5 split is best read as a substrate-and-elevation discontinuity rather than an arbitrary division of a continuous canopy population.

## 4.9 Mean water-table surface and flow field

The water table is a single mound, highest beside the bedrock ridge (mean head 13.32 m AOD at CEH14). It falls to the coastal head along Caernarfon Bay and to the river and lake levels inland (Figure 15). Left out one at a time, the wells are predicted with a median absolute error of 0.14 m in the mean state and almost no bias (−0.005 m). Flow runs outward from the high point. It runs south and south-west to Caernarfon Bay across the west and centre, north towards Llyn Rhos-Ddu from the slacks beside the lake, and east and south-east to the Afon Braint. The pattern barely changes with the state of the aquifer. The median gradient is 0.0071 in the wet state and 0.0062 in the dry, and the median flow direction at the slacks turns 4.7° between the two.

## []{#anchor-13}4.10 Water-balance residual at the wells

The water-balance residual is modelled losses minus modelled recharge at each well, calculated from the fitted coefficients. It closes tightly and has a small systematic negative offset. Its magnitude carries no spatial structure, but its sign tilts east--west (Figure 16). Residuals span −0.0114 to +0.0206 m/month about a median of −0.0044 m/month. Of the 65 reference wells carrying a residual, 61 lie inside ±0.01 m/month and 49 are negative; CEH14 has no Model B residual (implied base above ground). The cluster medians are negative except at C5 Coastal Forest (+0.0028 m/month), from −0.0030 m/month at C1 Lake Edge to −0.0062 m/month at C2 Dune. Residual magnitude is uncorrelated with position on either axis (Spearman ρ = 0.09 against Easting, p = 0.49; ρ = −0.10 against Northing, p = 0.43). The signed residual falls eastward (ρ = −0.35 against Easting, p = 0.005) but not with Northing (ρ = −0.10, p = 0.45).

Residuals exceed +0.02 m/month at 1 well, NW3 (+0.0206) in C2 Dune, and 16 of the 65 are positive. The next largest are CEH4 (+0.0117) and NW6 (+0.0103), both in C3 Western Residual. All three lie in the open dune rather than at the ridge. No C4 Main Forest well is positive. The largest negative residuals fall at the lake-edge wells CEH25 (−0.0114 m/month) and CEH27 (−0.0095 m/month), both in C1 Lake Edge. Two independent diagnostic tests on the monthly SSM residual both returned null results. One was a cross-correlation lag test for distance-dependent transport from the ridge; the other was a seasonal climatology test for unmodelled summer evaporative demand. No unmodelled flux is required to close the balance at any cluster.

## 4.11 The coastal component of long-term decline

Applied to each cluster's summer-minimum decline, the coastal-retreat gradient of the companion paper (Hollingham, 2026f) partitions the trend (Table 7). The gradient is a coast-edge deepening of about 26 mm/yr at 150 m from the shoreline, falling to zero over an inland reach of about 900 m. Eleven of C3 Western Residual's wells lie inside that reach, and coastal retreat accounts for most of its decline. At C4 Main Forest the coastal component is most of a decline the record does not resolve. C2 Dune has no well inside the reach and C1 Lake Edge one, so at both the whole of the decline is left unexplained rather than attributed to climate. C5 Coastal Forest, nearest the shore, is reported with a caveat: on four wells, coastal retreat accounts for about half of its decline (Table 7, note).
