# 5. Discussion

## 5.1 Geology, land cover and the cluster structure

The five hydrogeological clusters, resolved by hierarchical clustering of hydrograph dynamics, map onto the documented geological structure of the site. In the dendrogram, the top Ward merge (≈0.99) separates C4 Main Forest from the other 57 wells. The east--west division follows at ≈0.61. It separates the responsive eastern open dune (C1 Lake Edge, C2 Dune) from the buffered west (C3 Western Residual with C5 Coastal Forest). That contrast reflects the difference in subsurface stratigraphy described by Stratford et al. (2007). In the east, shallow sand over till and estuarine deposits constrains storage and drives flashy water-table responses. In the south-west, a deeper sand column supports a more buffered aquifer.

The mechanistic coefficients recover this divide independently of the clustering that defined it. They also resolve a gradient running through the open dune, rather than a simple binary. C1 Lake Edge is one extreme. It has the highest recharge sensitivity in the network (β₁ = 3.715), the fastest drainage (−β₃ = 0.354) and the shortest mean-reversion time in the network under Model B (2.1 months). This is a fill-and-drain regime, in which a shallow base promotes rapid lateral exchange directly with Llyn Rhos-Ddu. C2 Dune is larger than C1 and is the most representative open-dune unit (19 wells). It is the open-dune archetype between the end-members. Under Model B it has a still-high recharge sensitivity (β₁ = 3.500) and a drainage-dominated loss partition (45% of the mean loss), but a slower drainage decay (−β₃ = 0.167) and a longer mean-reversion time (4.4 months) than the lake-coupled C1. This reflects open dune without a direct lake connection. C3 Western Residual is the buffered opposite. Under Model B its recharge sensitivity sits between the other two open clusters\' (β₁ = 3.604), and it has the slowest drainage of the open clusters (−β₃ = 0.103) and the longest open-dune mean-reversion time (7.4 months). Here the deep aeolian sand attenuates both the rainfall pulse and its release. The forested interior fills slowly and drains most sluggishly of all. C4 Main Forest is the cluster geographically nearest the rock ridge, and the metamorphic bedrock outcrop forms its northern margin. That setting is reflected in the impeded drainage, which the record does not resolve well enough to quantify, and in the elevated atmospheric-draw coefficient relative to the other forested cluster (Section 5.2). It is revisited in the residual-field discussion (Section 5.4).

This gradient also bears on how C3 is best understood. Its membership is the most diffuse in the network. The great majority of its wells are gradationally assigned: they correlate almost as strongly with the C2 Dune centroid and with the coastal forest as with their own. It is also the open-dune cluster closest to both the plantation margin and the eroding Caernarfon Bay shoreline. C3 is therefore better read as the transitional, more strongly buffered south-western continuation of the open dune than as a discrete western block. It has a coherent central signature (the longest open-dune mean-reversion time and the most buffered open-dune response), but its boundaries grade into both the dune and the forest.

One parsimonious mechanism is consistent with the surface geology, though not directly observed here. A single estuarine-clay base crops out on the higher eastern and southern ground, where a thin overlying sand column produces the flashy C2 response. It dips beneath the surface toward Caernarfon Bay, where a thickening sand column buffers the C3 response. This would make C2 and C3 one dipping system rather than two substrate blocks.

The gradient within C3 is consistent with this. Across the 21 C3 wells that carry a coastal distance, recharge sensitivity β₁ rises inland (r = +0.752, p \< 0.001). The drainage coefficient carries the same sign without significance (r = +0.338, p = 0.13), and a β₃ gradient here holds only when the drainage base is fixed in advance, so it is not reported as a finding (Hollingham, 2026c, Section 7). Sₐ falls inland, from 0.40 at the south-western margin (CEH21) to 0.22 at the north-east (D38; r = −0.80, p \< 0.001). The response thus becomes more buffered toward the coast, which is the opposite of the flashier response a discharge boundary alone would produce. It grades toward the open dune at the cluster's inland edge. Because β₁ is recharge divided by storage, a single control accounts for the recharge and storage gradients together: a south-westward rise in near-surface storage (Sₐ).

The storage evidence points the same way and is independent of the coefficients. Within the open dune, the Sₐ values rise on a coherent planar trend toward the south-west (Section 4.5). That is the direction in which a dipping base would thicken the sand column. Coastal proximity, the plantation margin and the inferred clay dip all covary along the same south-western axis. This evidence therefore supports the transitional reading without isolating the clay dip as its sole cause. A cored or geophysical transect would be needed to test it directly (Section 5.7). Figure 17 maps the forest-interception drawdown propagating inland from the plantation; the companion paper maps the coastal-retreat reach (Hollingham, 2026f). Both place the C3 wells within their reach, while the C2 wells lie largely beyond them.

![](Pictures/100000010000074F000004F9345EE1F6.png){width="15.965cm" height="10.885cm"}

**Figure 17.** Illustrative forest reach. Forest-interception drawdown propagated inland from the plantation boundary by flow-weighted cost-distance (decay length λ ≈ 170 m, from C3\'s Sₐ and drainage coefficient combined with an assumed hydraulic diffusivity --- a literature conductivity, K = 6 m/day (Betson et al., 2002), and a nominal 5 m saturated thickness, the latter poorly constrained and plausibly larger; assumed edge deficit). The reach is a scaling estimate rather than a calibrated length: across the range reported for dune sand (K = 2--20 m/day) λ spans roughly 100--310 m, and across a 3--8 m saturated thickness 130--220 m, so it is stated here to the nearest tens of metres. The mapped pattern depends only on the reach being of order 200 m rather than of order 20 m or 2 km, which holds across that whole range, over the DEM hillshade with per-well drawdown values labelled. The C3 wells fall within the forest reach while the C2 wells lie largely beyond it --- drawdown falls from tens of millimetres near the plantation to under 1 mm at the easternmost C2 wells; the forest boundary, clearfell zone and Llyn Rhos-Ddu are marked. Drawdown magnitudes are illustrative of the reach rather than measured values; because the model represents canopy interception alone, its heads are a lower bound on the magnitude of the forest effect, and λ an upper bound on how far beyond the canopy that effect reaches.

[]{#anchor-14}The clustering (Figures 4 and 5) and the mechanistic coefficients (Figures 11--13 and Table 1) show the same structure. This is consistent with a partition that reflects the aquifer rather than the linkage method. The mean-reversion time (Figure 14) orders the clusters the same way. C1 Lake Edge recovers fastest and the forest interior slowest. C5 is distinct from C4 despite sharing the same canopy.

## []{#anchor-15}5.2 Substrate versus surface control: interpreting the coefficients

[]{#anchor-16}The two forested clusters are inferred to share the deep sandy substrate of the western block, and they carry the same Corsican pine canopy. Yet they segregate into distinct units. Resolving why is central to interpreting what the SSM coefficients measure.

Within the forest zone, elevation alone explains 93% of the variance in atmospheric draw (β₂ versus elevation, r = 0.964). C4 and C5 separate completely on this axis and on mean elevation (10.6 m versus 5.6 m). C4, on the elevated ridge flank, has a deeper water table and unsaturated zone, together with weaker drainage. We interpret this deeper profile as permitting stronger atmospheric draw. C5, on the lower coastal fringe, has a shallower water table and faster drainage. The measured contrast in water-table depth and coefficient behaviour is clear.

That interpretation has independent measured support at this site. Freeman (2008) recorded the water table beneath the Newborough plantation approximately 1.07 m below the open Warren (ANOVA p \< 0.001). She also recorded mean volumetric soil moisture there at roughly half the open-dune value. She attributed the moisture contrast to the loss of capillary contact between the upper soil layers and the water table where the water table is deeper. The forest zone therefore carries an unsaturated zone that is both thicker and drier, consistent with the coefficient contrast we recover.

The substrate explanation differs in confidence between the two clusters. For C4, the bedrock of the ridge outcrops within the forest, so the nature of the rock underlying the cluster is established. Its depth and extent beneath C4 are not known without coring. But the impeded drainage there is consistent with a shallow, irregular bedrock base close beneath the wells, an inference supported by the proximity of the outcropping ridge. The storage evidence within the plantation supports it directly. Across the fourteen forested wells, Sₐ falls with elevation (r = −0.93, p \< 0.001) and rises with distance from the ridge (r = +0.81, p \< 0.001). This is the pattern expected where a shallowing bedrock base thins the drainable sand column toward the outcrop. The relationship is robust to excluding the two anomalous ridge-flank wells (r = +0.79 against ridge distance with both removed). It is present in the uncorrected estimates as well as the corrected ones (r = +0.70, p = 0.005), so it is not an artefact of the canopy correction. For C5, the proposed more-uniform, deeper coastal sand is the weaker inference, resting on the coefficients and topography alone.

On that basis, the split is best read as a substrate-and-topographic-position discontinuity beneath a constant canopy, rather than an arbitrary division of a continuous population. The forest-interception drawdown footprint (Figure 17) occupies the same corner. The high atmospheric draw and the modelled drawdown reach therefore together describe one coherent forest signature. Both, however, are anchored to the same plantation-and-ridge zone, so their spatial agreement is mutual consistency rather than independent corroboration.

This finding clarifies a potential misreading of the cluster contrasts. The forested clusters carry the highest LCSC values in the network, which might be read as low aquifer drainability. But LCSC, like Sₐ, is an apparent storage: the fitted β₁ absorbs canopy interception alongside the true storage response. Part of the forest clusters' elevated LCSC therefore reflects the suppression of throughfall by the canopy, rather than a difference in the aquifer itself.

The Sₐ estimates bear on this directly. The uncorrected forest medians exceed the open-dune range. This is because the method attributes the full rainfall total to recharge, when in reality the canopy intercepts roughly a quarter of it. Once corrected for interception, C4's forest median (0.256) falls within the open-dune range (0.210--0.312). C5's (0.316) sits just above its upper edge, though C5's estimate is constrained by the physical-plausibility limit and is only weakly corroborative. The interpolated Sₐ surface shows no discontinuity at the cluster margins.

The effective storage inferred from the water-table response therefore varies smoothly and continuously across the site, stepping nowhere at the cluster margins. This is consistent with, though on these data not proof of, a well-mixed aeolian depositional history. The C4 Sₐ and the continuous Sₐ surface, rather than the ceiling-bound C5 estimate, carry the argument that the forest clusters' distinctive coefficient signature derives largely from a surface boundary condition (canopy interception) rather than from a different subsurface architecture.

A depth-dependent extension of the model lets atmospheric draw decline as the capillary fringe retreats from the root zone with increasing water-table depth. It was evaluated at cluster level as a diagnostic and is not adopted: the depth coupling it reports appears only when the drainage base is fixed in advance, and is therefore not a finding of this study (Hollingham, 2026c, Section 7). The standard fixed-β₂ model is used throughout, as an effective depth-averaged parameterization. The depth coupling and the lateral-drainage geometry contribute to the within-forest β₂ variation alongside substrate, but the dominant control on the cluster-level contrast remains topographic position and substrate rather than canopy. These within- and cross-cluster comparisons rest on the ordering of β₂ rather than on its absolute magnitude. The fitted β₂ values are OLS estimates biased somewhat high in absolute terms. They are reliable as rankings rather than as quantitative atmospheric-draw rates.

## 5.3 Recharge, loss and the water balance

[]{#recharge-loss-and-the-water-balance}Decomposed under identical climate forcing, the clusters differ markedly in recharge sensitivity, and the decomposition closes the mean balance to within 1.7% of total losses at every cluster. How the loss divides is less certain. Under Model B drainage takes the larger share at C3 and C5 (56% and 61%), and atmospheric draw at C1 and C2 (62% and 55%). C1's drainage rate, β₃, is nonetheless the largest in the network, reflecting rapid lateral exchange with the lake. At C4 Model B does not identify the drainage term, so the Main Forest's split is not established on this record.

The suppression has two components. Interception removes a fraction of rainfall at the crown. In addition, the profile beneath the canopy is measurably drier, so a larger storage deficit must be satisfied before the remainder reaches the water table; Freeman (2008) recorded roughly half the open-dune volumetric soil moisture beneath the plantation. Her felled clearing plot carried a water table statistically indistinguishable from the open Warren. This indicates that the second component is a consequence of the canopy rather than an independent property of the forest zone.

Model B holds β₃ positive, and β₃ is significant at four clusters. At C4 it is not (p = 0.45), so Model B does not identify the Main Forest's drainage, or its share of the loss, on this record.

Two cautions attach to the recharge term. First, the model is fitted to heads alone, and its intercept absorbs any constant offset. In an open-boundary system the recharge coefficient can therefore absorb unmeasured boundary fluxes (Young, 2011; Knotters and van Walsum, 1997). β₁·P should not be read as a direct measure of local precipitation reaching the water table. Second, the atmospheric-draw coefficient is an effective parameter. Thornthwaite PET is an energy-based demand index, and it does not define a reference surface in the manner of Penman--Monteith. β₂ therefore folds transpiration, interception, storage and depth coupling into a single scaling between atmospheric demand and water-table response, and a formal crop-coefficient decomposition does not apply. Both cautions are consistent with the substrate interpretation above. The coefficients are diagnostic of behaviour. Their physical decomposition requires the independent Sₐ and depth-coupling evidence assembled here.

## 5.4 Boundary conditions and the water-balance residual field

[]{#anchor-17}The near-closure of the water balance at the cluster mean also holds in space. The residual at the wells is modelled losses minus modelled recharge, from the fitted coefficients. It lies within ±0.01 m/month at 61 of the 65 reference wells carrying a residual. Its magnitude carries no gradient across the site, and its sign falls only weakly eastward. Its cluster medians span −0.006 to +0.003 m/month. A positive residual would mark a location where measured rainfall-driven recharge does not fully account for the observed water level, implying an unmodelled input. One well, NW3 in the open dune, carries such a residual above +0.02 m/month. The 16 positive residuals are largest in the open dune (NW3, CEH4, NW6) rather than at the ridge, and no C4 Main Forest well is positive. The largest negative residuals fall at the lake edge (CEH25, CEH27). On this evidence, no ridge-derived lateral input is required to close the balance, and the residual field provides no positive support for one.

Two further diagnostics constrain what the record could have detected had such an input been present. Two independent diagnostic tests both returned null results: a cross-correlation lag analysis for distance-dependent transport from the ridge, and a seasonal climatology analysis for unmodelled summer evaporative demand. The cross-correlation null is itself qualified by sampling frequency. Monthly observations are an order of magnitude coarser than the days-to-weeks transit times expected for fracture-flow input from a metamorphic bedrock ridge. A real ridge-derived lag could therefore be invisible at this resolution. The null result bears on what the present record can resolve, not on whether the mechanism is operative.

The seasonal phase of the residual narrows the field further. The residual peaks in winter and early spring at the great majority of wells, and at none in summer. That is inconsistent with any vertical-flux parameterization error: systematically underestimated summer PET, an incomplete canopy-interception correction, or any under-resolved summer evaporative demand. All of these would peak in summer, when those fluxes are active. The phase is consistent instead with either a winter-phased nonlinear recharge mechanism or ridge-derived lateral input arriving during the months of greatest rainfall.

A cluster-stratified version of the same climatology shows mean winter-minus-summer residual contrasts of +8.6 mm in C3 (p\<0.001), +5.4 mm in C4 (p=0.068, marginal) and −0.3 mm in C5 (not significant). The C3 \> C4 \> C5 ordering and the magnitude of the C3 signal together rule out canopy-interception over-estimation as the sole driver of the winter--summer contrast, since the largest signal sits in a cluster with no canopy.

The residual pattern is real and reproducible, but its mechanistic attribution is unresolved. This is the appropriate stance for a lumped-parameter framework. The residual field is a structural diagnostic of where the three-term balance is insufficient. It is not a quantified map of lateral flux, because it also absorbs nonlinear soil-moisture dynamics, coefficient sensitivity and any systematic PET bias.

## 5.5 Long-term decline away from the coast

Coastal retreat accounts for part of the decline near the shore (Section 4.11; Hollingham, 2026f). The decline it does not explain is the subject of this section.

The decline observed away from the coast, in the clusters that carry no gradient component or a negligible one (C2 and C1), is a candidate for further mechanistic work. At least two non-exclusive climate drivers are candidates. What the gradient regression cannot supply is the quantity those drivers would be fitted to. The panel absorbs the spatially uniform forcing through the cumulative-water-balance covariate. A constant offset trades off exactly against the trend contribution that covariate carries, so no residual far-field rate is isolated here (Section 4.11). The mechanisms below are accordingly motivated by the decline the network records, not by a fitted background. Climate forcing, separately measured over the station record, is the leading candidate for that decline.

The horizon of the decline is also bounded. Ranwell's levelled 1951--53 readings provide the comparison. Set against them, the open slacks he measured stand today within about a decimetre of their mid-century level once the climate of the two periods is allowed for (−0.09 ± 0.10 m at the six sites beyond the coastal reach, over sixty-six years; Hollingham, 2026d, §5.7.9). The decline this record resolves is therefore an excursion within a near-stationary century, not the visible part of a longer trend.

The deterioration is concentrated in the summer months. This is consistent with rising evaporative demand under the documented post-2013 summer warming (Figure 3), acting through the atmospheric-draw term as elevated potential evapotranspiration. That route is, if anything, understated by the forcing. Thornthwaite carries the heat index in its denominator and constructs it from the same temperatures, so the formula partly cancels its own response to warming. Across the station record, a 7.2% rise in mean annual temperature (0.73 °C between 1931--1960 and 1996--2025) produced a rise of only 3.0% in mean annual PET, an elasticity of 0.42. The evaporative demand implied by the temperature record therefore exceeds the demand the model was forced with.

A reduction in effective recharge is also plausible. One example is a shift in the within-month distribution of rainfall, expressed as a declining recharge sensitivity. The two routes sit differently within the framework. The warming signal enters directly through the model's potential-evapotranspiration forcing. A sub-monthly rainfall redistribution, by contrast, is invisible to a monthly model and would surface only as an apparent decline in recharge sensitivity. The framework makes the network-wide signal visible. On the present analysis, it does not resolve which route dominates, or what share of the observed decline either accounts for. Both are noted as forcings the characterization exposes, not results the paper establishes.

## 5.6 Predictive skill and transferability

[]{#predictive-skill-and-transferability}The practical contribution of the framework rests on the benchmarking result. In one-step diagnostic mode the state-space and traditional linear models are nearly indistinguishable, because each prediction is corrected by the previous observation. The distinction emerges under iterative simulation. There the SSM achieves a median Nash--Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.83 against the linear model's 0.38, and returns a positive iterative NSE at all 64 wells fitted on the comparison window, against 53 for the linear model. The head-dependent drainage term pulls the level back towards its mean, which prevents the cumulative drift to which the linear model is prone. Out of sample, fitted on one side of January 2018 and run freely across the other, the SSM's median NSE is 0.79 forward and 0.78 in reverse (Hollingham, 2026c, Section 4.2).

That skill extends beyond the fitted record, with one limitation that matters for any projection. Driven by the station record from 1930 on its present-day coefficients, with no refitting, the per-well model reproduces the seasonal water-table cycle of Ranwell's 1951--53 readings (Ranwell, 1959; median NSE 0.83 with each hindcast's mean offset removed). Over the drier decade of 1989--96, however, it puts the water table 0.18 m too high at the median well (Hollingham, 2026c, Sections 4.4 and 5.1). The model forecasts within the recorded climate; in a lastingly drier one it is likely to understate the fall.

The spatial pattern of the gain is itself a diagnostic. The largest improvements concentrate in the lake-proximal eastern aquifer, where head-dependent drainage is strongest. The smallest occur in the forest interior, where weak drainage makes the storage term nearly dispensable. The improvement map therefore indicates which parts of the aquifer are governed by head-dependent drainage and which approximate a linear climate response. It is a structural characterization obtained without any invasive measurement.

This is the basis for transferability. The framework requires only four fitted parameters per well and monthly rainfall and temperature from a single climate station. It does not require hydraulic-conductivity measurements, aquifer-thickness surfaces or lateral-flow modelling. These are precisely the parameter-sparsity constraints that produced calibration difficulties for an earlier distributed-model effort at this site (Betson et al., 2002).

The head-dependent drainage term is the methodological choice that enables this. It captures the head-dependence of the drainage response without calibrating the drainage geometry, and because the fitted intercept absorbs the reference level, no drainage base has to be chosen at a new site or transferred between sites (Hollingham, 2026c, Sections 2.2 and 5.3). Where the record does not identify the drainage term, as in the forest interior, the fit says so rather than returning a value set by the choice of base. With monthly rainfall and temperature from a nearby station, any coastal dune aquifer with a manual dipwell network can be parameterized in the same way. The diagnostic syntheses demonstrated here (the recession half-life, the ΔNSE gain and Sₐ together, the coefficient atlas, the residual field) follow directly from that parameterization.

One supplementary step reaches outside this core. Rendering the forest-interception drawdown as a physical reach in metres (Figure 17) requires a hydraulic diffusivity. For this, a single literature conductivity (K ≈ 6 m/day; Betson et al., 2002) and a nominal saturated thickness are assumed, the latter uncertain by a factor of two or more. These enter only that illustrative reach length. The core parameterization, the diagnostic syntheses above and the empirically fitted coastal reach (Hollingham, 2026f) all remain free of conductivity and thickness inputs. The forest reach is accordingly an order-of-magnitude diagnostic rather than a calibrated prediction.

## 5.7 Framework limitations

[]{#discussion}[]{#framework-limitations}The framework's strengths and its limits are two sides of the same design choice. It fits a lumped mass balance independently at each well and interpolates the results geometrically, so it does not resolve lateral groundwater flow. The interpolated coefficient and head surfaces are aggregators of point responses, not a physical flow model. They cannot represent cluster-to-cluster hydraulic coupling, the lateral redistribution of localized recharge perturbations, or the diffusive response of the aquifer to a change in boundary flux. The affinity analysis and the Darcy field show that the clusters are connected along a continuous downslope drainage pathway. Whether a signal originating in one part of the aquifer propagates to another at magnitudes below the framework's resolution therefore cannot be answered here. That is a question for a calibrated continuous-flow model.

The critical unknowns for such a model are the very quantities the present framework avoids. One is hydraulic conductivity, currently constrained by a single tracer test (6.0 m/day; Betson et al., 2002). The other is aquifer thickness, inferred from a handful of borehole logs across the site. A measured K would also tighten the only K-conditioned output of the present framework, the forest-drawdown reach length in Figure 17. As noted in Section 5.6, however, all other framework outputs (SSM coefficients, WTF Sₐ estimates, substrate-gradient interpretation, coastal-retreat regression and residual field) are K-independent and would not change with a measured K. The priority field measurements to enable a flow model are slug tests at representative wells per cluster and a ground-penetrating-radar survey of aquifer thickness. These would also support an independent vadose-zone test of the canopy-driven recharge-suppression signal.

The same campaign would test the structural interpretation of the C3 transition (Section 5.1). A south-west to north-east transect would resolve the depth to the estuarine-clay base, carrying the Caernarfon Bay coastal-retreat rate as a covariate. It would establish whether the eastward-to-south-westward buffering gradient reflects a single dipping clay base (one thickening sand column) rather than two distinct substrate blocks. It would also separate that structural control from the confounded coastal and plantation-margin influences.

Several further limitations qualify specific results. The monthly measurement resolution cannot isolate individual storm events. The Sₐ estimates therefore conflate gravity drainage with capillary-fringe release, and are upper bounds on storage, not the specific yield of the sand, rather than point estimates (Healy and Cook, 2002; Scanlon et al., 2002). Thornthwaite PET is a temperature-and-daylength index whose absolute magnitude is uncertain. The framework's internal consistency does not depend on it, but absolute flux estimates derived from it do.

The magnitude of the water-balance residual shows no spatial structure at the wells, and its sign only a weak east--west tilt, but its monthly series carries a reproducible winter-phased seasonal pattern. As discussed, the attribution of that pattern between a genuine lateral flux and a modelling artefact is unresolved.

The clusters describe the modern record. Grouped on their 1989--96 readings, the CCW wells did not reproduce them (Section 4.3). The difference lies with the warren wells near the sea: then they moved with the inland warren; today they move with wells on their landward side, near the forest edge. That could mean the ground changed between the two periods, or it could reflect a short early record with many readings at the bottom of the pipe, and the record cannot say which. The clusters are therefore not applied to 1989--96, and gaps are filled from cluster-mates only within the modern record, where the method was tested.

Finally, the water table follows the ground closely only once the DEM is smoothed to the scale of the dune ridges (r = 0.92 at 300 m, against 0.76 at native resolution). Topography is therefore a proxy for the regional form of the water table, co-determined with it by the underlying till and bedrock architecture. It is not a proxy for local flow paths, and DEM-derived surface routing is not a guide to groundwater flow direction.

# 6. Conclusions

This study sets out a parameter-sparse state-space framework for characterizing the hydrogeological architecture of a coastal dune aquifer from routine monitoring data. It demonstrates the framework across 88 dipwells and 21 years of monthly records at Newborough Warren. The principal conclusions are:

1.  **Five hydrogeological clusters govern site hydrology. **The Pearson affinity audit of hydrograph similarity independently supports cluster assignment for 91% (60 of 66) of reference-network wells (Section 4.3). The cluster-level contrasts in SSM coefficients, drainage timescales and apparent storage provide mechanistic substantiation. The five units resolve as a responsive eastern block (C1 Lake Edge, C2 Dune), a buffered Western Residual (C3), and two forested clusters distinguished by topographic position and inferred substrate. C4 Main Forest, on the elevated ridge flank, has the higher atmospheric draw of the two forested clusters, and drainage the record does not identify. C5 Coastal Forest lies on the lower coastal ground. Within the forest zone, elevation alone explains 93% of the variance in atmospheric draw, which identifies position and elevation, rather than canopy, as the dominant within-forest control.
2.  **Within the modern record, a well's cluster-mates are a better guide to its missing months than the climate model.** The nearest cluster-mate put back hidden spring levels with a median miss of 0.041 m, against 0.139 m for the SSM on climate alone, including in 2006--08, when the water table stood higher than the climate explains. The clusters are not shown to have held in 1989--96: grouped on their readings then, the 12 CCW wells matched today's clusters no better than chance (adjusted Rand index 0.03). They are not carried back to that period (Section 4.3).
3.  **The aquifer's storage varies smoothly, without discontinuity at the cluster margins; the cluster contrasts are surface-mediated.** Once corrected for canopy interception, the C4 forest Sₐ falls within the open-dune range. The interpolated Sₐ surface shows no discontinuity at the cluster margins. The C5 estimate sits at the upper edge of that range and is the least reliable in the network, so it is treated as weakly corroborative. The forest clusters' distinctive coefficient signature therefore derives largely from a surface boundary condition, canopy interception suppressing recharge, rather than from a different subsurface architecture.
4.  **The model closes the water balance and substantially improves forecast skill.** The three-term model closes the monthly water balance to within 1.7% of total losses at every cluster. This is a property of the fit rather than independent evidence. The split between drainage and evapotranspiration is not identified from heads alone. At the median well it is 45% drainage under Model B and 31% from an independent water balance (36--55% across its storage bracket). The model achieves a median iterative Nash--Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.83 against 0.38 for a traditional linear model, with a positive iterative NSE at all 64 wells fitted on the comparison window against 53. The spatial pattern of the improvement is itself a non-invasive diagnostic of where head-dependent drainage governs the aquifer.
5.  **The water balance closes on average, and the magnitude of its residual shows no spatial structure at the wells.** Residuals lie within ±0.01 m/month at 61 of the 65 reference wells carrying one. Their magnitude carries no gradient across the site, and their sign only a weak east--west tilt. One well, NW3 in the open dune, exceeds +0.02 m/month, and the largest positive residuals fall in the open dune rather than in the forest. No unmodelled lateral flux is required to close the balance at any cluster. A cross-correlation lag test and a seasonal climatology test on the monthly residual likewise return null results for ridge-derived input. The monthly sampling interval is, however, coarse relative to the transit times expected of fracture flow, so the nulls bound what this record can resolve rather than excluding the mechanism. The residual field is a structural diagnostic of model adequacy, not a quantified flux map.
6.  **Coastal retreat is removed before the decline is read. **Near the eroding shore a coastal-retreat gradient, analysed in a companion paper (Hollingham, 2026f), accounts for most of the western dune cluster's summer-minimum decline and about half of the coastal forest's. Away from the coast the decline is left unexplained rather than attributed to climate.
7.  **The framework is transferable.** It characterizes aquifer architecture (storage, recharge sensitivity, storage decay and flow structure) from manual dipwell records and a single climate station. It does so without coring, hydraulic testing or calibrated continuous-flow modelling. It needs no site-specific drainage base: the fitted intercept absorbs the reference level, so nothing has to be swept or transferred (Hollingham, 2026c). Its principal limitation is the converse of this strength. As a geometric aggregator of point responses, it cannot resolve cluster-to-cluster hydraulic coupling. That would need a calibrated flow model, and the hydraulic-conductivity and aquifer-thickness measurements it requires.

[]{#conclusions}The companion paper (Hollingham, 2026b) quantifies the hydrological consequences of the dune-scraping and plantation-clearfell interventions undertaken at the site, within a before-after-control-impact framework.

# Declaration of generative AI and AI-assisted technologies in the manuscript preparation process

During the preparation of this work the author used Anthropic's Claude (successive Claude Opus and Claude Fable models, accessed through the Claude desktop application) for substantial drafting and editing of the manuscript text: composing prose from the author's analytical outputs and decisions, structuring and restructuring sections, and correcting the text against the study's committed analytical outputs. The conception and design of the study, the twenty-one-year manual dipwell record on which it rests, the analytical decisions, and the interpretation of the results are the author's own. Numerical values in the manuscript were verified against the committed outputs of the analysis pipeline, and a decision log records the methodological and editorial calls made by the author during the work. After using this tool the author reviewed and edited the content as needed and takes full responsibility for the content of the published article.
